title: Ingredient Alternatives & Substitutions
description: Reliable swaps for common ingredients, plus a dedicated halal substitute list for recipes that traditionally call for a haram animal ingredient -- every swap below uses chicken, beef, mutton, lamb, duck, fish/seafood, or a plant-based alternative.

items.notes: Chicken bacon is the closest match for streaky, smoky bacon strips in breakfasts, salads, and sandwiches.
Chicken ham (pressed, cured chicken) slices and cooks the same way as regular ham in sandwiches and quiches.

items.ingredient: Guanciale / pancetta (cured pork jowl or belly)
items.notes: Used in Carbonara and Amatriciana; beef or chicken bacon gives a similar salty, rendered-fat base.
Beef chorizo is widely available and carries the same smoked-paprika flavour.
Bresaola is a real, traditional air-dried beef product from Italy, not an imitation -- a genuine like-for-like swap.
Widely sold pre-made; works identically on pizza.
Beef bratwurst holds its shape and snap on the grill the same way.
Beef tallow behaves closest to lard in pastry for flakiness.
Check that beef gelatin is halal-certified; agar-agar is a reliable plant-based setting agent for jellies and desserts.

alternatives: Soy sauce + a squeeze of lime
items.notes: Most fish sauce is naturally halal (fermented fish and salt); check the label if unsure.

alternatives: Grilled chicken skewers with garlic-herb butter
items.notes: No true equivalent exists; the garlic-parsley-butter sauce is the part worth recreating, served instead over chicken.
Chicken wings take on the same garlic-butter or curry preparations frog legs are typically cooked in.
Cooking wine is commonly considered acceptable in this collection since the alcohol content largely cooks off during simmering or baking -- use freely where a recipe calls for it.

alternatives: 1 cup milk + 1 tbsp lemon juice or vinegar, rested 5 minutes
items.notes: Curdles slightly, mimicking buttermilk's tang and acidity for baking.
Won't whip into peaks, but works for cooking and baking.
Nearly interchangeable in both flavour and texture.
Best for savoury cooking; baking texture changes slightly with oil.
Any plant milk works in most savoury and baking applications.

alternatives: 1 tbsp ground flaxseed + 3 tbsp water per egg
items.notes: Best for cakes, muffins, and quick breads; less reliable for meringues or soufflés.
Mix well; restores the moisture and flavour brown sugar adds.
Arrowroot gives a clearer thickened sauce than flour.

alternatives: 1/4 tsp baking soda + 1/2 tsp cream of tartar per 1 tsp
items.notes: Use immediately, as the reaction starts right away.

alternatives: 1 cup all-purpose flour + 1.5 tsp baking powder + 1/4 tsp salt
items.notes: Standard self-rising flour substitution ratio.

alternatives: 1 cup all-purpose flour minus 2 tbsp, plus 2 tbsp cornstarch
items.notes: Sift together well for an even, lighter crumb.

alternatives: Instant yeast (equal amount, skip proofing step)
items.notes: Instant yeast can be mixed directly into dry ingredients.
Coconut aminos are sweeter and less salty; use slightly more.

alternatives: Apple cider vinegar + a pinch of sugar
items.notes: Balances the mellow sweetness rice vinegar has.
Works in hummus and dressings, though the flavour becomes nuttier.

alternatives: White miso + chilli paste + a touch of sugar
items.notes: Approximates the sweet-savoury-spicy balance of gochujang.

alternatives: Soy sauce + a splash of vinegar + a pinch of sugar
items.notes: A reasonable stand-in when the anchovy-based original isn't available.
Toasting regular breadcrumbs adds back some of panko's crunch.
Dried herbs are more concentrated; add earlier in cooking to rehydrate.
Combine roughly 1 small onion and half a garlic clove per shallot.
Best for cooked dishes rather than raw applications.
Cashew cream is the closer match for dairy-free cooking.
Not identical, but captures the citrusy-aromatic quality.
